label: Revision continuity is fileKey-based: the first call creates a file, every later diagram of the same work and every revision passes that fileKey, and one board holds the work.

The retry rule refuses to assume failure means nothing landed: read the target before retrying, retry only when the diagram is absent, and ask the user to look for a first-call draft because there is no fileKey.
Rollback is scoped to what this write created: delete only those nodes and connectors, after the user agrees, and stop if a node to delete was not created by this write.

Mismatch repair reports measured counts, deletes the created nodes and regenerates under the same fileKey only after agreement, because a second write beside the first duplicates; after two attempts, stop and ask.
Adobe independently caps regeneration at two attempts on one complaint and then asks what is wrong, converging with the packet on a bounded retry.
Read-back compares board to model by count, label, endpoints, direction and type extras, and a screenshot read is labelled visual because a picture cannot prove which nodes a connector joins.
The rubric checks the board visually for stretched shapes, cut labels, overlaps with existing content and any post-generation movement, a separate check from the structural read-back.
The plan is fixed before the write because a board in the wrong plan is visible to that plan members as soon as it lands, a confidentiality gate no corpus source has.
Extension failure is explicit partial success: the diagram stands and the reply reports what landed and what did not.

Revision is all-or-nothing at diagram granularity: generated nodes may never be moved, so a bad layout is fixed only by splitting or reshaping, while mermaid-jam preserves moved positions and diagram-codebase regenerates only affected diagrams.
The fj fallback changes read-back semantics because each edge label is a separate text node counted as a label, never a node, so one model yields different counts per route.
With no route the packet refuses a stand-in file, naming what is missing and offering the checked model instead, where every corpus alternative produces an image, a board or Mermaid text.
The 9-node and 12-connector budget with split-not-shrink and ordered cuts is the strictest density rule in the corpus, and the no-move rule is why it protects legibility before the write.
